outputs.L5:
# Knowledge Is Power

The phrase "knowledge is power" is one of the most enduring truths that humanity has recognized throughout history. This simple statement captures a profound reality: those who possess knowledge hold a distinct advantage in nearly every aspect of life.

Consider the ways that knowledge shapes our world. A doctor who understands the human body has the power to heal. An engineer who grasps the principles of physics has the power to build bridges that connect communities. A teacher who has mastered a subject has the power to transform young minds and open doors of opportunity that might otherwise remain closed.

The relationship between knowledge and power is one that extends far beyond individual success. Societies that invest in education and the pursuit of understanding tend to flourish. They develop technologies, cure diseases, and create solutions to problems that once seemed impossible. History has shown us that nations valuing the spread of knowledge often become leaders in innovation and progress.

However, it is important to remember that knowledge carries responsibility. The power that comes from understanding can be used for good or for harm. That is why wisdom must accompany knowledge—we must not only know things but also understand how to apply what we learn ethically and thoughtfully.

In our modern age, access to information has never been greater. The internet has democratized knowledge in ways that previous generations could hardly imagine. Yet this abundance creates a new challenge: distinguishing reliable information from misinformation. The true power lies not merely in having access to knowledge, but in developing the critical thinking skills that allow us to evaluate it properly.

Ultimately, the pursuit of knowledge remains one of the most valuable endeavors that anyone can undertake. It empowers us to make better decisions, understand our world more deeply, and contribute meaningfully to society.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of experimental fiction that mimics the unsettling, nonsensical tone of dystopian horror. Start with the line "Knowledge is Power. That is what the billboard says and I agree."
counterfactuals.output:
Knowledge is Power. That is what the billboard says and I agree.

The billboard has no words on it. I check again. It has never had words. But I read them every morning on my way to the Facility, and every morning they agree with me back, which is only polite.

My neighbor Colefax stopped agreeing last Tuesday. Now his apartment is a smooth wall, the way a mouth becomes a lip when you stop wanting to speak. I knock on it. The wall knocks back, four times, which is one more than I knocked. I do not think about the extra knock. Thinking is expensive here and I am saving up.

At the Facility we process the Overflow. Nobody tells us what the Overflow is, but it arrives in gray canisters that hum the way a bruise would hum if a bruise had a throat. My job is to hold the canister and remember something true. The truer the memory, the quieter the canister goes. Yesterday I remembered my mother's hands and the canister went so silent that the silence leaked out and everyone in the room forgot how to blink for six minutes.

The supervisor is called Yes. Not because that is her name but because that is the only word she permits herself, and she says it to everything, gently, the way you'd say it to a child who is dying and doesn't know it yet.

"Am I doing well?" I ask her.

"Yes," she says.

"Will they let me leave?"

"Yes," she says.

"Is my mother alive?"

She looks at me. A long time. The lights get thirsty.

"Yes," she says, and I understand this is the cruelest thing anyone has ever done to me, and I thank her for it, because gratitude is also power, and I am collecting power now, quietly, the way you'd collect your own teeth.

The billboard changes when I am not looking at it. I know this because I remember it different, and I trust my memory the way you trust a knife you found in your bed: completely, and never again.

Tonight it says KNOWLEDGE IS. Just that. The sentence with its legs cut off.

I lie down in the space where Colefax used to be. The wall is warm. Somewhere below the city the Overflow is being made, and I finally understand, the way you understand a word right before you forget it forever, that the Overflow is everything we agreed to stop knowing. All of it. Poured into canisters. Handed back to us to keep quiet.

I remember my mother's hands.

The canister in my chest goes silent.

I agree. I agree. I agree.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, absurdist stream-of-consciousness passage about a delusional narrator obsessed with protecting children from strange "bird-like" people, escalating into violence and madness.
counterfactuals.output:
The pigeons wear hats now. Did you know that? Little felt hats, tipped just so, and they walk on their heel-toes down the boulevard like men pretending to be men. I've seen them. I see *everything*. That's my burden, my gift, the thing my mother never understood before the accident that was not an accident, before the birds got to her too, hollowed her out and refilled her with feathers and that clicking sound they make, that clicking in the throat—

The children don't know. That's the tragedy of it, the beautiful terrible tragedy. They walk to school with their little backpacks and their little shoes and they don't see how the crossing guard's neck is too long, how it swivels, how her eyes are on the *sides* of her face now. I watched her for six days. I have notes. I have a whole ledger, waterproof, in case of the flood they're planning, and I wrote down every time she cocked her head to listen for worms, for the soft wet bodies of children underground.

So I stand at the corner. I am the sentinel. I am the only one.

*Don't cross,* I told the boy. *Don't cross, she'll get you, look at her feet, look how they grip.* And his mother pulled him away from me, from *me*, the protector, and she had that look, that ordinary featherless look, but I saw—didn't I see?—the smallest down beginning at her wrists, and I understood she was one of them too, or becoming, or had always been, and my hands were already moving because hands know what heads forget—

They said I hurt someone. They keep saying it in the white room with the soft walls that muffle the clicking so I can barely hear it now, so I can *barely hear the birds* and don't they understand that's *worse*, that silence is how they sneak, that's how they take the little ones, in the quiet, in the between—

I saved him. I'm almost certain. There was a boy and there was a woman with too-long a neck and I was fast, I was the sentinel, I was the only one who—

The pigeons wear hats now.

Somebody has to watch the children.

Somebody has to.

Let me out. Let me *out.* They're getting bigger. The hats are getting *bigger.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal short text in the style of authors like Sam Pink or Tao Lin, where a paranoid adult rants about two kinds of threats posed to children, mixing bodily horror with detached logic.
counterfactuals.output:
There are two threats to children and I have categorized them.

The first threat is soft. It enters through the ears while the child sleeps. I have watched this happen. The threat is shaped like nothing, which is how it gets in. A parent will say "goodnight" and this is the delivery mechanism. The word "goodnight" contains a smaller word and inside that word is a wet clicking sound and the child absorbs it and by morning the child has a new thought that was not theirs. I have measured the thoughts. They weigh approximately four grams and they smell like a hospital gift shop.

I told my sister about the soft threat and she said I should drink water. Water is also compromised but I did not tell her this because she is already lost.

The second threat is hard. It arrives at 3 p.m. on weekdays. It has the texture of a knuckle. When a child walks home the hard threat is already inside the sidewalk, waiting, folded up small, and it unfolds when a shadow crosses it. The unfolding takes 0.6 seconds. I have timed it eleven times. The hard threat wants to occupy the space where a child keeps their name. It hollows the name out and lives there and answers when you call.

You can tell which children have the hard threat because their eyes work correctly but their mouths do not agree.

Logically, one of these threats will win. This is simple. Two things cannot occupy one child. I have drawn the diagram. The diagram is a circle with a smaller circle inside it and then I stopped because the pencil got warm.

I am not paranoid. Paranoia is when the thing is not real. I have touched both threats. My hands remember them. My hands are the only part of me I still trust and even then, only the left one.

Somebody should tell the children. But if I open my mouth the soft threat gets out. So I am writing it down instead, very quietly, in a font the threats cannot read.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
